/environment/2026/oct/20/jackdaw-north-s.headline: Heat pumps and insulation would cut UK living costs more than new oilfields, study suggests
/environment/2026/oct/20/jackdaw-north-s.excerpt: Insulating Britain’s homes and investing in heat pumps would do more to cut the cost of living, create jobs and boost the UK’s economy than drilling for new oil, research suggests. The government’s £15bn warm homes plan, currently under threat of cuts as ministers seek budget savings, would slash £1bn a year from household energy bills across the UK, concentrated on those on low incomes, according to research by the thinktank E3G. It would also provide a £1.6bn yearly boost to the economy, and about 50,000 new jobs spread across thousands of small businesses. The Rosebank oilfield, west of Shetland, would create about 1,100 direct and indirect jobs, the analysis found. The jobs would be concentrated in the North Sea and in two companies, one of them – Equinor – an overseas investor. A decision on whether to give the green light to the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea was “imminent”, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, said on Wednesday. A decision on Rosebank would take a little longer, she said. Labour promised in its 2024 election manifesto to halt new licensing for oil and gas, but Jackdaw and Rosebank could be exceptions because they were already in the licensing system. Equinor previously estimated 3,500 jobs would be created at peak for Jackdaw and Rosebank combined.
/environment/2026/oct/20/jackdaw-north-s.trail: Warm homes plan would create 50,000 jobs, compared with about 1,100 for Rosebank oilfield, thinktank finds

/environment/2026/oct/20/jackdaw-north-s.headline: North Sea gasfield decision likely delayed until after Holborn and St Pancras byelection
/environment/2026/oct/20/jackdaw-north-s.excerpt: A decision on approving the controversial Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea is to be delayed until later this autumn, with the Greens accusing Labour of hiding their position before the crucial Holborn and St Pancras byelection. Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, had been poised to give her recommendation to approve the Jackdaw field off the coast of Aberdeen next week. However, multiple Whitehall sources say the decision is not expected to be made in the remaining few days before the House of Commons goes into recess on Tuesday for party conference season. The delay means the announcement is unlikely to come before Holborn and St Pancras constituents vote in a high-profile byelection on 8 October, in which the Green party leader Zack Polanski is the candidate vying against Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali in Keir Starmer’s former seat. Polanski has criticised the government over signals that it will press ahead with Jackdaw despite the hottest ever summer caused by the climate crisis. After his selection, Polanski said Labour has “started the campaign with an act of dishonesty and betrayal”. “They are clearly going to allow new drilling in the North Sea but want to keep it under wraps during a byelection where they know the public want tougher action on climate, not backsliding. “Labour talks about change, but this is change for the worse.
/environment/2026/oct/20/jackdaw-north-s.trail: Greens accuse Labour of hiding position to avoid criticism before contest, in which Zack Polanski is standing

/environment/2026/oct/20/jackdaw-north-s.headline: Jackdaw gasfield set to be approved by ministers this month, sources say
/environment/2026/oct/20/jackdaw-north-s.excerpt: Ministers are poised to approve a controversial new gasfield in the North Sea this month, according to government sources, and are considering approving a major oilfield later this year. Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, will give her recommendation to approve the Jackdaw field off the coast of Aberdeen as soon as next week, according to people close to the decision, and the formal approval could follow a week after. Meanwhile, officials are looking for ways to make sure any proceeds from the separate Rosebank project – if it is approved – go towards clean energy projects, as happens in Norway. Officials have not yet finished their analysis of Rosebank’s environmental impact, but some close to the process believe they will soon decide the project should be approved. Both projects have become emblematic of the government’s commitment to the North Sea, with green campaigners calling for them to be abandoned while the US president, Donald Trump, urges the prime minister to open them up. A spokesperson for the energy department said: “The North Sea remains a vital national asset, supporting jobs, growth and the UK’s energy security.
/environment/2026/oct/20/jackdaw-north-s.trail: Energy secretary could recommend new North Sea drilling next week, as ministers also consider approval for Rosebank oilfield

/environment/2026/oct/20/jackdaw-north-s.headline: Labour ‘could lose up to 50 seats’ to Greens if new drilling in North Sea approved
/environment/2026/oct/20/jackdaw-north-s.excerpt: Labour could lose dozens of seats to the Green party if the government allows new drilling in the North Sea, according to internal research shared with the Guardian. Green party analysis suggests up to 50 Labour MPs, including Andy Burnham’s key ally Louise Haigh, could lose their seats at the next election if the government fails to make urgent climate action a priority or allows new drilling for oil and gas in the North Sea. The research found that voters in these key Labour v Green seats want bold action to tackle the climate crisis, which has contributed to record heatwaves, devastating wildfires and crippling droughts this summer in the UK – and say Labour MPs will pay the price if the demands are not met. Rachel Millward, a deputy leader of the Green party, said: “If Labour won’t be swayed by the science or the moral imperative to leave all fossil fuels in the ground, perhaps they will listen to the polling. “The data is clear: voters want more from our government on climate change, and they certainly don’t want our new prime minister to back away from his party’s bare minimum commitments.” Labour dismissed the claims, pointing out that since Burnham took office the number of seats the Green party is projected to win at the next election had fallen from 20 to seven.
/environment/2026/oct/20/jackdaw-north-s.trail: Greens say analysis shows government failure to take bold climate action could lead to big gains for party at election

/environment/2026/oct/20/jackdaw-north-s.headline: From grey water to cool spaces: 10 climate crisis policies Britain needs right now
/environment/2026/oct/20/jackdaw-north-s.excerpt: From record-smashing temperatures, wildfires, hosepipe bans and thousands of premature deaths, the climate crisis has left its mark across the summer of 2026. Tackling the root cause – the burning of fossil fuels – and ending the crisis will take years. So will fixing the UK government’s calamitous failure to protect lives and livelihoods against the long-predicted affects of global heating. But the climate emergency is right here, right now, and here are 10 policies that Andy Burnham’s government should consider announcing urgently. 1. Reject drilling licences for the Jackdaw and Rosebank oil and gasfields This would be a vital and confidence-boosting sign that the UK is committed to putting a rocket-booster under the clean, green and very fast-growing economy of the 21st century, not the fossil-fuelled one of the last. It would also give diplomatic weight to the UK as it works internationally to cut emissions and end the climate crisis. The supposed benefits of approving the North Sea oil and gasfields are mostly fantasy. They will have no impact on UK energy prices – oil and gas are commodities whose price is set by international markets. As the UK Energy Research Council says: “Assertions that drilling the North Sea will provide energy resilience and affordability in the face of current fuel price shocks are a delusion.” As for jobs, the licences would support very few – again, unlike the growing green economy.
/environment/2026/oct/20/jackdaw-north-s.trail: Rejecting North Sea drilling licences and protecting nature are just some measures Andy Burnham must implement to ready country

/politics/2026/oct/20/senior-reform-offi.headline: Farage claim that £5m was reward for Brexit was ‘not press office line’, close aide says
/politics/2026/oct/20/senior-reform-offi.excerpt: Nigel Farage undermined his own claims that a £5m gift was for security when he referred to the money as a reward for Brexit, according to one of his closest aides. The apparent admission came in undercover footage seen by the Guardian in which Dan Jukes says that it is “priced in” for Farage to profit from politics. The footage raises fresh questions about the party leader’s statements that the gift was solely for security purposes. The Reform UK leader is awaiting the outcome of a parliamentary watchdog investigation into whether or not the £5m from the crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne, first revealed by the Guardian, should have been declared under parliamentary rules. Farage told the Sun on 14 May: “And this [£5m] was given to me on an unconditional basis, completely unconditional basis. But frankly, it was given as a reward for campaigning for Brexit for 27 years.” Now, previously unpublished footage from the undercover reporting group Verbatim, shared with the Guardian, has revealed a conversation between Jukes, a longtime close aide of Farage, and an undercover reporter. “That was not the line to take from the press office,” Jukes said of Farage’s admission that the funds were a political reward, appearing to suggest that it was an on-air accident.
/politics/2026/oct/20/senior-reform-offi.trail: Exclusive: Undercover footage of Dan Jukes raises fresh questions about Reform leader’s statement that £5m gift was for security

/politics/2026/oct/20/senior-reform-offi.headline: Reform clears its own officials of breaking party funding laws despite police investigation
/politics/2026/oct/20/senior-reform-offi.excerpt: Reform UK has cleared two of its senior officials of breaking laws that ban foreign donations, despite the matter remaining under police investigation. The party published a 27-page report of an internal inquiry finding that Dan Jukes, Nigel Farage’s press adviser, and James Orr, its head of policy, had not breached funding rules. Party sources said they intended to pursue legal action against the undercover reporting group Verbatim, whose footage led to the investigation and was broadcast by Channel 4 News. However, Labour said the report was a “whitewash” given it was undertaken by the party’s legal secretary, Adam Richardson, a barrister with a longstanding association with the party, and Tom Waterhouse, its general secretary. Labour also said it was not credible for the party to distance itself from the scandal by claiming Orr and Jukes, two of Farage’s top team, were just contractors. Police have been investigating potential offences under electoral law since the broadcast in early September, saying they would widen an existing special inquiry relating to donations made to Reform. Jukes, 30, and Orr, 47, will remain suspended by the party while the police inquiry continues. Jukes and Orr were filmed talking about a scheme in which a US donor paid for three polls with favourable narratives for Reform, costing more than £30,000. Donations from overseas sources are not allowed under political funding laws.
/politics/2026/oct/20/senior-reform-offi.trail: Internal inquiry exonerates Dan Jukes and James Orr, who were filmed talking about scheme involving US donor

/politics/2026/oct/20/senior-reform-offi.headline: Burnham’s reopening of Brexit debate is ‘biggest boost in my career’, says Farage
/politics/2026/oct/20/senior-reform-offi.excerpt: Nigel Farage has claimed that Andy Burnham has given him “the biggest boost in my career” by reviving the Brexit debate, which the Reform UK leader said had reopened a “huge flank” to his party. The prime minister’s pledges to the Labour conference and admission on Wednesday that rejoining the EU was among options the government would look at had put “put me back into the debate”, he said. Looking tanned and relaxed before his party’s first major rally since its conference last month, Farage indicated to reporters that he was relishing a return to the playbook that he and others deployed during the 2016 referendum. Dismissing polls showing that as much as 59% of the public favoured rejoining the EU, Farage told the Guardian: “Of course they do, until you tell them it’ll cost 25bn quid a year, until you tell him it’ll mean joining Schengen [the area of Europe that has open borders], until he tells them it will mean actually having to recommit to joining the euro. “Remember that the leavers haven’t made their arguments since 2016. The ‘remoaners’ have made their arguments every single week. I mean, do you know what? I actually think that Burnham has made a very big political mistake here.” Farage was speaking before a rally in the South Yorkshire city of Doncaster, the first of a series Reform is holding around Britain on the theme of what the party would do in its first 100 days of government.
/politics/2026/oct/20/senior-reform-offi.trail: Reform UK leader tells supporters PM’s move has ‘opened up a huge flank to us’

/politics/2026/oct/20/senior-reform-offi.headline: UK politics increasingly funded by billionaires as mega-donations surge
/politics/2026/oct/20/senior-reform-offi.excerpt: British politics is increasingly being funded by individual billionaires with a wave of mega-donations having flooded into UK political parties over the past two parliaments. A total of £179m has been donated by wealthy individuals since 2019, research reveals. The figures from the IPPR thinktank show how big money is playing an ever more influential role in Westminster, with a particular rise in mega-donations of more than £1m. The research found that contributions from individual donors have accelerated since the Brexit party received £10m from the Thailand-based billionaire Christopher Harborne and the Liberal Democrats were given £8m by David Sainsbury, the supermarket tycoon, who has now returned to Labour. Between 2001, when donation records began, and 2018, the total donated by individuals giving more than £1m averaged £3.9m a year. But between 2019 and 2025, that figure rose to £13.1m a year, almost three-and-a-half times as much, and far outstripping what would be expected with inflation. The research found 72% of all £1m-plus donations from individuals since records began had come since 2019. Guardian analysis found that in some years, such as 2023, almost £7 out of every £10 in reported private donations to political parties came from wealthy companies or individuals who gave more than £1m in a calendar year.
/politics/2026/oct/20/senior-reform-offi.trail: Exclusive: A total £179m has been donated by wealthy individuals since 2019, research reveals

/politics/2026/oct/20/senior-reform-offi.headline: Reform UK activists squabble over Farage’s plan for £72m donations
/politics/2026/oct/20/senior-reform-offi.excerpt: For Nigel Farage, the £72m lavished last week on his party by the crypto billionaire donors Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne finally places Reform UK on a level playing field with its political rivals. The donations are the largest received by a UK political party since declarations became required in 2001 and led to warnings Farage was aiming to “buy” his way to power, with a row still raging over whether they are legal. Yet among Reform’s grassroots, the fattening of party coffers comes with challenges of its own, with some activists less than impressed by Farage’s announcement that the money would be used to hire 400 campaign managers in target constituencies. “We need more activists to knock on doors NOT managers,” one posted on a Facebook group used by Reform activists, where the sentiment was not unusual. Another party member, and former candidate, told others he was “puzzled” by Farage’s announcement, adding that the campaign managers would need an army of volunteer doorknockers. “Those campaign managers will rapidly learn that they can’t get nearly enough volunteers to do that. Are Reform planning actually to pay them too, not just the managers?” he asked. “And what happens to the ordinary branch members currently serving as campaign managers having been elected by their membership to that role?” Substantial spending by Reform on professional organisers is already under way.
/politics/2026/oct/20/senior-reform-offi.trail: Crypto billionaires’ £72m will be used to hire campaign managers and professional staff in target constituencies

/world/2026/oct/20/us-has-resumed-sharin.headline: Nato increases Black Sea deployment amid escalating deadly Russian attacks
/world/2026/oct/20/us-has-resumed-sharin.excerpt: Nato is deploying additional military assets to the Black Sea amid the recent deadly escalation of Russian attacks on merchant shipping, as five more vessels were attacked on Tuesday. Russia’s military said it ⁠struck three cargo vessels in Ukraine’s ⁠port of Reni and two ⁠other cargo vessels en route ‌to ‌Odesa. Russia’s targeting of vessels taking grain and other agricultural cargoes from Ukraine’s ports – central to the country’s economy – have brought the conflict to Nato’s borders, with a new high-risk designation used by the London shipping insurance market now covering all of the Black Sea save for the territorial waters of Romania, Bulgaria and Turkey. With a sharply rising death toll among civilian seafarers that has made Black Sea routes the world’s most dangerous, Nato announced the ⁠defensive military alliance would add more surveillance assets in the region. Nato’s spokesperson, Allison Hart, said: “Today, Nato ‌ambassadors met in ‌the North Atlantic Council to discuss security in the Black Sea. Nato has already strengthened our posture along the eastern flank, including with counter-drone ⁠capabilities. Nato will be sending additional assets to the region, including ‌support for surveillance, reconnaissance, and forensics.” The deployment will include maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems, drones and intelligence personnel. There is mounting anxiety about the increasing overspill from Russia’s war on Ukraine and the potential for further friction with Nato.
/world/2026/oct/20/us-has-resumed-sharin.trail: Mounting anxiety as Russia’s war on Ukraine reaches Nato’s borders with targeting of vessels transporting agricultural cargo

/world/2026/oct/20/us-has-resumed-sharin.headline: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy claims US deliberately delaying interceptor missile deliveries to Kyiv
/world/2026/oct/20/us-has-resumed-sharin.excerpt: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the US is deliberately delaying deliveries of interceptor missiles to Ukraine, deepening a public spat with Donald Trump. Speaking to US senators on Monday, the Ukrainian president claimed that “the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles” already paid for by European countries under the prioritised Ukraine requirements list (Purl) program. According to Zelenskyy, the shipment is awaiting the signature of the US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth. A White House official, who spoke to the Washington Post on condition of anonymity, said the US “continues to play a constructive role in speaking to both sides in working towards bringing the war to an end”. Zelenskyy also said several European countries were ready to transfer Patriot interceptor missiles from their own stockpiles but were still awaiting US approval. “All of this suggests that some political decision has been made to slow down the support for us,” he said in remarks released by the Ukrainian presidency. The ‌Post reported the Trump ⁠administration had not approved ⁠the ⁠transfer of the interceptor ‌missiles ‌to Ukraine. Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for soaring fuel prices that are a major issue in coming US midterm elections. “To be honest, I think it’s time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine,” Trump said on Monday.
/world/2026/oct/20/us-has-resumed-sharin.trail: Ukrainian president tells US senators the delayed missiles have already been paid for by European countries, amid growing rift. What we know on day 1,700

/world/2026/oct/20/us-has-resumed-sharin.headline: Ukraine war briefing: Trump accuses Zelenskyy of not wanting to end war as feud rumbles on
/world/2026/oct/20/us-has-resumed-sharin.excerpt: Donald Trump has defended his decision to waive some sanctions on Russia, while once again accusing Volodymyr Zelenskyy of not wanting to end the war. “My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table,” the US president wrote on Truth Social. “Zelenskyy doesn’t care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him … he doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did,” he added. Trump’s remarks come after he signed an executive order on Friday putting on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy. Earlier on Sunday, Zelenskyy had thanked the Trump administration for resuming intelligence sharing between the two countries, but maintained the US had intentionally throttled its Starlink satellite internet access to send a “message” to Kyiv, write Andrew Roth and Sam Jones. Lithuania said Russia was likely behind an attempted arson attack on a company hosting communication hardware for Starlink satellites. Prime minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius made the claim on broadcaster LRT after authorities discovered flammable liquids at the company in question. Sinkevicius said the firm, whose location he did not mention, houses “nine satellite antennas to guarantee the Starlink connection, which of course supports and assists Ukraine”.
/world/2026/oct/20/us-has-resumed-sharin.trail: Trump defends decision to waive some sanctions on Russia; Lithuania foils attack on Starlink site; Kyiv hits another oil terminal. What we know on day 1,699

/world/2026/oct/20/us-has-resumed-sharin.headline: Intensifying drone attacks on ships in Black Sea bring war ever closer to Nato shores
/world/2026/oct/20/us-has-resumed-sharin.excerpt: The first the crew of the Bulgarian ferry Dioscuria knew of an attack on a cargo ship in their country’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea in the early hours of 6 October was a distant explosion 70 miles off the coastal town of Byala. The Turkish-owned Alfa Watan, heading for the Romanian port of Sulina, had been struck by suspected Russian air and naval drones. Arriving on the scene, Dioscuria found an overturned lifeboat and lifejackets in the water. There was no sign, however, of Alfa Watan’s crew of 10. Six days later drones struck another ship off the coast of Bulgaria, HS Dignity. Eleven crew members died. By Thursday, the attacks had encroached on Romania’s airspace and territorial water. Two chemical tankers, Wine Trader and Yara J, were attacked and left burning. Seven more sailors were missing. The attacks on six ships in 10 days – the Able and Chelsea-3 were also hit – marked a dramatic escalation in a maritime conflict that is pressing on Nato’s borders. While global attention has focused on the risks for sailors travelling through the strait of Hormuz, in recent months it is the Black Sea that has emerged as the more dangerous passage, with more sailors lost in a week and a half than US service members killed in the entire Iran war. The maritime insurer and risk analyst Ambrey has warned that there is no end in sight to the threats to Black Sea cargo shipping, including grain and oil, and that insurance prices for passage of the waters have rocketed.
/world/2026/oct/20/us-has-resumed-sharin.trail: Six attacks in 10 days by suspected Russian drones mark dramatic escalation in maritime conflict

/world/2026/oct/20/us-has-resumed-sharin.headline: Ukraine war briefing: Trump’s sanctions waiver is a ‘60-day pause’ to analyse economic impact, says Rubio
/world/2026/oct/20/us-has-resumed-sharin.excerpt: US secretary of state Marco Rubio has said that US President Donald Trump’s waiver of sweeping sanctions and tariffs on Russia would be a 60-day pause to “analyse” their impact on the global economy. Rubio said also no one at the White House ordered the slow down of the speed of Ukraine’s access to Starlink to prevent it from being used on drones flying faster than 100mph, referring to Starshield, the military version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite internet network. “The president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy,” Rubio said, noting that the economic restrictions involved a number of countries, not just Russia. Pointing to high energy prices and the Iran war, “we need that period of time to sort of study all this and figure out what the right combination is,” he said. Trump’s abrupt decision to waive sanctions on Russia days before they were to take effect drew outrage Saturday from members of Congress, which had overwhelmingly passed the legislation. Republican Senator Rick Scott said it was clear Russia was the aggressor, and said the US had “to do everything we can to put economic pressure on Russia”. On social media, fellow Republican Thom Tillis described the move as “beyond irresponsible” and a capitulation “to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine”.
/world/2026/oct/20/us-has-resumed-sharin.trail: Ukraine’s Zelenskyy expects Trump to lift more sanctions against Russia. What we know on day 1,698

/uk-news/2026/oct/21/firefighters-growin.headline: The UK wildfire investigators: ‘If someone has used a match, chances are you’ll find it’
/uk-news/2026/oct/21/firefighters-growin.excerpt: From the scorched heathlands of the New Forest to the smouldering valleys of south Wales and burned-out homes in Stourbridge, an extraordinary summer of wildfires has left its mark across Britain. To most of us, these charred landscapes may look like pure devastation, but to a trained wildfire investigator they are full of clues. Heat-scorched leaves can become frozen in position, preserving evidence of the wind direction as the fire passed through. Soot or staining on rocks, the pattern of fallen grass and bracken, and even how those stems have burned, provide further information about how the fire itself moved. By combining such clues, investigators can work backwards through a fire, progressively narrowing their search to a likely area of origin, then to a smaller patch within it. “At this point you’re on your hands and knees, looking in great detail,” said Andy Elliott, the UK’s only serving fire officer trained in specialist wildfire origin. “If, for example, somebody has used a match, or if a firework was the cause, the chances are you’ll find it.” Yet, surprisingly few people are trained to read a burnt landscape in this way. While fire crews routinely record a probable cause, a 2023 Forestry Commission report warned that these judgments were generally made by personnel with limited or no specialist training, leaving their accuracy “open to scrutiny”.
/uk-news/2026/oct/21/firefighters-growin.trail: Scientists are racing to understand how fires behave to predict and prevent them as hotter summers create tinderboxes

/uk-news/2026/oct/21/firefighters-growin.headline: ‘Real struggle’ to tame New Forest blaze as UK set for hottest summer on record
/uk-news/2026/oct/21/firefighters-growin.excerpt: The battle to contain a large wildfire spreading across the New Forest will go on for several days, experts have said, as wind changes and a desiccated landscape fuel the flames. Smoke billowed above the deserted A31 road, the main tourist route into the New Forest national park where tens of thousands of families are on holiday, late on Tuesday while a helicopter flew above the blaze. Firefighters at the scene said they were trying to contain several hotspots across the more than 100 hectares (247 acres) of dried heathland as winds swirled over the area. Roads, including the A31 dual carriageway, will remain shut until at least Thursday, Hampshire’s fire service said, adding that “significant” repairs were needed to the surface, barriers and fencing. One source at the scene said: “They are really worried that as they dampen down the top, the peat underneath is still alight and spreading the fire. It is too dry, too windy, and it is a real struggle.” July was the busiest month on record for wildfires, the National Fire Chiefs Council said on Tuesday. Its services have responded to 966 wildfires this year, including 458 in July alone. Parts of England are bracing for a fifth heatwave of the summer this week as climate breakdown makes extreme heat, drought and wildfires more likely. The Met Office said on Tuesday that the UK was on course for its hottest summer on record by average temperature.
/uk-news/2026/oct/21/firefighters-growin.trail: Key tourist route closed and residents rallying round as battle against wildfire expected to go on for several days

/uk-news/2026/oct/21/firefighters-growin.headline: Wildfire near Sizewell nuclear plant causes ‘total devastation’ to Suffolk landscape
/uk-news/2026/oct/21/firefighters-growin.excerpt: A wildfire near Britain’s biggest nuclear power station has caused “total devastation” to one of the UK’s most important landscapes, as fire crews said the situation remained “dynamic”. More than 100 firefighters have been battling the blaze on Dunwich Heath, near Leiston, on the Suffolk coast since Wednesday evening. The fire service said on Friday afternoon the situation was stabilising but remained a “major incident” that was “dynamic and potentially changeable”. Firefighting efforts have included a helicopter capable of dropping 1,000 litres of seawater on each pass and six London fire brigade appliances. The fire has burned approximately 150 hectares (370 acres), equivalent to 210 football pitches, of vegetation and forest on Dunwich Heath and the Minsmere nature reserve, which are both protected sites and home to some of the UK’s rarest species. Russell Clement, the general manager for the National Trust on the Suffolk coast, said the fire had “torn through” the entire Dunwich Heath National Trust reserve. Clement said the reserve was now “unrecognisable” and the fire had caused “total devastation” to one of the UK’s most important coastal heathland landscapes. Hilary McGrady, the National Trust’s director general, on Friday launched an emergency fundraising appeal for the restoration of the heathland, a rare “lowland heath” that is visited by 100,000 people each year. McGrady said: “We are looking at total devastation of a beloved and important landscape.
/uk-news/2026/oct/21/firefighters-growin.trail: Emergency crews say situation remains ‘dynamic’ as more than 100 firefighters battle Dunwich Heath blaze

/australia-news/2026/oct/21/no-bail-bren.headline: Brendan Nugent stares in silence as a court hears about his alleged attack on Helen Haines
/australia-news/2026/oct/21/no-bail-bren.excerpt: The media pack was so large when it descended on Wangaratta magistrates court on Wednesday morning that not everyone could fit in the courtroom. They spilled into the hallway, forced to try to log in remotely or pick up clues from afar. Everyone was hoping to catch a glimpse of Brendan Nugent, who was arrested less than 100 metres away two days earlier after allegedly ramming the independent MP Helen Haines twice in a targeted attack outside her electorate office. That office remained shuttered on Wednesday and eerily quiet, but for dozens of flowers and cards that had been left for Haines as she remains in hospital in a critical condition, with surgeons fighting to save her other leg. The 43-year-old’s motive remains under investigation, and a mystery to the dozens of reporters crammed into courtroom two. He said nothing during his brief hearing, and stared straight ahead, looking downcast in a grey jumper, with a long beard. He did not request bail, and will remain in custody until a committal mention on 4 February next year. The magistrate, Allison Vaughan, noted Nugent had mental health and neurological concerns, and that it was his first time in custody. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here His lawyer, Chirag Patel, said Nugent suffered from idiopathic transverse myelitis – a rare neurological condition caused by inflammation of the spinal cord, which can result in muscle weakness, pain and bladder dysfunction.
/australia-news/2026/oct/21/no-bail-bren.trail: There were no family or friends inside the Wangaratta magistrates court to support the accused, a 43-year-old from Tarrawingee

/australia-news/2026/oct/21/no-bail-bren.headline: A chaotic few minutes and a beloved MP’s life in the balance: a Victorian community grapples with the unfathomable
/australia-news/2026/oct/21/no-bail-bren.excerpt: It sounded like a car accident – as though someone had unintentionally backed into another vehicle on the quiet main street in the north-east Victorian city of Wangaratta. Across the road, Cody Lepoidevin had been helping a customer in the High Country RoadHouse – an outdoor store directly across from the office of his local federal MP, Helen Haines. It was about 3.35pm on Monday. Haines had finished her drive back to the office from a sod-turning event in Mansfield – passing state forests and farmland that make up much of the scenery of the region along the way. /society/2026/oct/21/weight-loss-in-midd.headline: Does GLP-1 use result in significant hair loss?
/society/2026/oct/21/weight-loss-in-midd.excerpt: About 20 million people across the US, UK, and EU are taking GLP-1 receptor agonists like tirzepatide and semaglutide (Ozempic or Mounjaro are common brands) for weight loss and type 2 diabetes. As their use has surged, we’re learning more about their side-effects. One that’s been getting a lot of attention from researchers lately: hair loss. In one survey of people who take these medications, 20% of respondents experienced hair shedding, although the lack of high-quality data from a randomized, controlled trial to assess this side-effect makes it difficult to know exactly how common it is. While GLP-1-related hair loss is often temporary and reversible, it’s significant enough that some patients hesitate to take drugs they would otherwise benefit from using. Here’s what you need to know. What kind of hair loss are people seeing on GLP-1s? Most people who take GLP-1 drugs don’t have hair loss. However, those who do often notice it within the first year, usually peaking a little before the 12th month. They’re usually experiencing one of two types of hair loss, says Lynn Petukhova, a geneticist at New York University who studies hair loss disorders. The most common type is a stress-related condition that dermatologists call telogen effluvium, where a stressor pushes an unusually large share of hair follicles into their resting phase. During this stage, the affected hair ceases to grow – and after two to three months, it falls out.

/society/2026/oct/21/weight-loss-in-midd.headline: From ‘Ozempic breath’ to hair loss: sorting the science from the hype about weight loss jabs
/society/2026/oct/21/weight-loss-in-midd.excerpt: They suppress your appetite so you never feel hungry FALSE “GLP-1 medications mimic Glucagon-like peptide-1 – one of the hormones involved in appetite regulation. It doesn’t completely suppress hunger, but it is powerful,” says Dr Federica Amati, nutrition lead at Imperial College School of Medicine and author of The Appetite Reset. “The medicine is about 1,000 times stronger than what we naturally produce from our gut,” she explains. As food passes through the gut, cells called L-cells sense the nutrients, which sparks the production of the GLP-1 hormone. Without the drugs, these bursts of GLP-1 production last a few minutes. “It’s a bit like a sparkler. In comparison, the drugs are like a bonfire that roars for a week,” says Amati. Because the GLP-1 hormone stays in your body for longer if you are on the drugs, you feel fuller faster and your appetite gets suppressed, but you will eventually get hungry. They can cause gastrointestinal issues TRUE “Nausea, constipation, diarrhoea, bloating and vomiting are well-recognised side-effects,” says Dr Adrian Brown, associate professor and specialist dietitian at University College London. “They tend to occur during dose escalation, and most symptoms improve over time.” Eating smaller meals, staying hydrated and limiting fatty foods can help. “One of the best ways to prevent these side-effects is to prepare your gut, liver and pancreas before you start taking the medications,” says Amati.

/society/2026/oct/21/weight-loss-in-midd.headline: ‘I’m sick of her talking about it’: 11 readers share how GLP-1s have affected their relationships
/society/2026/oct/21/weight-loss-in-midd.excerpt: As GLP-1 use continues to rise in the US and the UK, people’s bodies are being reshaped – as are their relationships. “Relationships tend to develop a sense of equilibrium and predictability over time,” says Dr Lindsey Berisha, a licensed clinical psychologist who has worked with clients using GLP-1s for over 10 years. “When one partner undergoes a significant change, it can shift that equilibrium, and even positive change can create uncertainty for both partners.” Berisha says that her clients who use GLP-1s often report feeling relieved that they are no longer consumed with thoughts of food. These users often develop more self-compassion, she says, as they realize what they previously interpreted as a failure or lack of self-control was a legitimate biological drive and food preoccupation that made life harder for them. “This shift can often be more impactful than the weight loss itself,” she says. But these changes can elicit mixed reactions from partners, family and friends, says psychologist Dr Rachel Goldman, ranging “from being supportive to feeling insecure, left behind, or worried that the relationship itself is changing”.

/society/2026/oct/21/weight-loss-in-midd.headline: ‘Who knows what they’re taking?’: people risk the gray market for the newest weight-loss drug
/society/2026/oct/21/weight-loss-in-midd.excerpt: About two years ago, Henry, who is 6ft 3in, weighed 210lb, which meant he was only slightly overweight, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention body mass index. Still, the thirtysomething who lives in the Pacific north-west had hypertension, sleep apnea and body image issues, so he started taking the weight-loss drug Ozempic. While he dropped pounds, he experienced constipation, a common side-effect, so he wanted to try retatrutide, another peptide which not only targets GLP-1 but two other hormone receptors as well. He had read about it in the news and on Reddit forums. The problem is, the US Food and Drug Administration has not approved the drug, so Henry bought it online from sellers in China. Henry, who did not want his last name used, is among a growing number of people dissatisfied with the revolutionary weight-loss drugs that can be obtained legally with a prescription and have instead turned to the gray market to purchase retatrutide, which is manufactured by the pharmaceutical company Eli Lilly and is being studied in clinical trials. Physicians see the drug as a promising potential solution for people struggling with obesity, but strongly warn patients that they are seriously risking their health by using it without oversight from doctors and government regulators. Yet these warnings often go unheeded.

/society/2026/oct/21/weight-loss-in-midd.headline: People’s bodies are changing in the age of Ozempic. How are we meant to talk about it?
/society/2026/oct/21/weight-loss-in-midd.excerpt: In the age of Ozempic and people being open about plastic surgery, discussion about people’s bodies is rife. At the same time, nobody seems quite sure how to talk about them, as shown by recent coverage of celebrities like Ariana Grande. It is a fraught topic. We asked eating disorder experts for guidelines to follow when talking about other people’s bodies, and how to do so without doing harm. Why does it feel particularly hard to talk about bodies right now? For experts in the field of eating disorders, the current ambivalence makes sense. “There’s a whiplash moment we’re stuck in,” says Dr Tom Hildebrandt, director of the Center for Eating and Weight Disorders at Mount Sinai hospital in New York. The body positivity movement of the 2010s saw a mainstream push to “accept all body sizes, shapes and types”, says Hildebrandt. Then, with the explosion of GLP-1s, progress toward body acceptance “took a hard right turn”, he says – once again, “the media went through its idealization of weight loss”. The vocabulary is different than it was before. Now, the focus is on “optimizing” one’s body and appearance, says Dr Ulrike Schmidt, professor of eating disorders at King’s College London. The deluge of social media posts has only exacerbated the confusion and made it feel impossible to escape body discourse.

/world/2026/oct/21/hastings-british-muse.excerpt: Our journalists often draw connections between seemingly disparate issues or events to give people a fuller grasp of how things interrelate. But not every story can convey the scope and complexity of today’s algorithmically warped reality. One of the Guardian’s regular cartoonists has managed this feat by drawing inspiration from a medieval embroidery made almost 1,000 years ago. Edith Pritchett was asked by her editors on the Guardian’s Saturday magazine to draw a modern-day version of the Bayeux tapestry, the 11th-century artwork that has been capturing imaginations this month as it goes on public display in the UK for the first time since its creation. Her updated version was included as a pullout poster in the print edition of the Guardian last weekend and also published as a special scrollable digital feature. Whereas the original Bayeux tapestry tells the story of the events leading up to the Norman conquest of England in 1066, Edith’s take on it depicts today’s battles with online trolls, social media addiction, the manosphere, AI agents and a natural world ravaged by fossil fuels. But her version is more than just a topical reimagining: it gives the viewer a genuine feel for how the different components of today’s dystopia amplify each other.
